newsitem.title: ISRAEL: A spark could ignite Palestinian frustrations.
newsitem.headline: A spark could ignite Palestinian frustrations.

text.p: Israeli bulldozers carving into a hill in Arab East Jerusalem to build new homes for Jews have stoked Palestinian emotions to near boiling point where any spark could ignite an explosion, Palestinians said on Wednesday.
"When I saw the bulldozer moving towards the mountain, I felt as if it was tearing up my heart," said 20-year-old Ramzi Salha, a university student from the Gaza Strip.
"We want to go down to the streets to protest. But we feel that the (Palestinian) Authority does not want anything like that," he said.

Israel sent its bulldozers to work on Tuesday, breaking ground for the construction of 6,500 houses on Jabal Abu Ghneim, a forest of pine trees which Israelis call Har Homa, on the southern outskirts of Jerusalem.
Only a handful of Palestinians and Israeli peace activists protested at the arrival of the bulldozers under the glaring lights of television cameras from around the world.
The Palestinian Authority allowed street protests on Wednesday in areas under self-rule but stopped demonstrators from reaching Israeli military checkpoints around the self-rule areas.
The West Bank and Gaza Strip were largely quiet on Wednesday, with only peaceful protests in some PLO-ruled cities, despite calls by an Islamic militant group for all-out revolt.

"I do not expect a flare-up like the one that happened after the (Jerusalem) tunnel. But I do see people stoking their pain, anger and frustration inside them," said Zuhair al-Dib'i, a Palestinian mosque preacher.

"The question is when will people release those feelings," Dib'i said. The last eruption of violence, over Israel's opening of a tunnel in East Jerusalem in September, claimed the lives of 61 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers.

Khalil al-Shikaki, a prominent Palestinian analyst, said that the tunnel, near an Islamic shrine, had tugged at the spiritual and religious feelings of Palestinians. But the new settlement is more a political issue that does not directly affect their lives, he said.
"Of course the new settlement creates serious tension on the streets. But we are not on the verge of an explosion," Shikaki said.
"The situation is so delicate that even television pictures or a call by the Palestinian leadership could touch off protests," he said.

But many Palestinians, who regard Arab East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state, say the building on an area captured in the 1967 Middle East War is an attempt by Israel to "judaise" and change the demographic status of the city before final status talks which were due to start on Monday.
Israel has rejected international criticism of the settlement, saying it was part of the Jewish state's capital.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has asked Palestinians to shun violence during protests against the settlement, which the PLO says would be like a wall dividing the southern part of the West Bank from the north.
Palestinians followed news of the Israeli construction, but most went about their business normally on Wednesday.
"Israel is trying to fool the world by showing that it is a victim of Palestinian violence," said Bassem Abu Baker, a 32-year-old merchant in Jenin.
"It is trying to justify its muscle flexing and threats and to divert attention from its actions," he said.
